title: Unit 9 test: Parametric Equations, Polar Coordinates, and Vector-Valued Functions
author: bc-tests-extensions
directions: Original Liminal practice. Section I Part A and Section II Part B are without a calculator; the other parts require a graphing calculator. Show supporting work and justify conclusions in free response. Angles are in radians. Use exact answers without a calculator and three decimal places for calculator work unless a question specifies otherwise. Report raw practice points only.

figures.alt: A curved arc goes from (0, 0) through (−1, 1) to (0, 2). These three points are labeled t = −1, t = 0, and t = 1, respectively; no direction arrows are supplied.

parts.title: No calculator
parts.directions: Select one answer for each question.

items.prompt: The displayed parametric curve has x = t^2 − 1 and y = t + 1 for −1 ≤ t ≤ 1. As t increases, which ordered sequence describes its motion?
items.rationale: Substitute t = −1, 0, and 1 in that order to get (0, 0), (−1, 1), and (0, 2).

distractorNotes.B: This starts at t = 0 instead of t = −1.
distractorNotes.C: This ignores the intermediate parameter value.

items.prompt: For x = t^2 and y = t^3 with t > 0, what is d^2y/dx^2 at t = 1?

distractorNotes.A: This differentiates dy/dx with respect to t but does not divide by dx/dt.
distractorNotes.C: This divides the second t-derivatives instead of using the parametric rule.
distractorNotes.D: This reports d^2y/dt^2 instead of d^2y/dx^2.

items.prompt: For x = t^3 − 3t and y = t^2, where does the curve have horizontal and vertical tangents?
choices: Horizontal at t = −1 and 1; vertical at t = 0.
Horizontal at t = 0; no vertical tangents.
Horizontal at t = 0; vertical at t = −1 and 1.
No horizontal tangents; vertical at t = −1 and 1.
items.rationale: dx/dt = 3t^2 − 3 and dy/dt = 2t. A horizontal tangent needs dy/dt = 0 with dx/dt ≠ 0; a vertical tangent needs the reverse.

distractorNotes.A: This interchanges the numerator and denominator conditions.
distractorNotes.B: dx/dt vanishes at ±1 while dy/dt does not.
distractorNotes.D: dy/dt vanishes at 0 while dx/dt does not.

items.prompt: A particle has velocity vector v(t) = (2t, 3t^2) and position r(0) = (2, −1). What is r(1)?
items.rationale: Integrate velocity componentwise: r(t) = (2 + t^2, −1 + t^3). Therefore r(1) = (3, 0).

distractorNotes.B: This gives displacement rather than position.
distractorNotes.C: This adds endpoint velocity to the initial position.
distractorNotes.D: This omits the initial vertical coordinate.

items.prompt: At one instant, a planar particle has velocity (3, 4) m/s and acceleration (−2, 1) m/s^2. What is the instantaneous rate of change of its speed?
items.rationale: The rate of change of speed is (v·a)/|v| = [3(−2) + 4(1)]/5 = −2/5 m/s^2.

distractorNotes.A: This is acceleration magnitude, not the signed rate of change of speed.
distractorNotes.B: This reverses the sign of the velocity–acceleration dot product.

items.prompt: A point on r = 2 sin θ has θ = π/6. What are its Cartesian coordinates?
items.rationale: At θ = π/6, r = 1. Thus x = r cos θ = √3/2 and y = r sin θ = 1/2.

distractorNotes.A: This swaps sine and cosine in the coordinate conversion.
distractorNotes.B: This uses radius 2 instead of the actual radius 1.
distractorNotes.D: This treats the positive radius as negative.

items.prompt: For the polar curve r = 2 + cos θ, what is the slope dy/dx at θ = π/2?
items.rationale: r = 2 and r′ = −1. Then dx/dθ = r′cos θ − r sin θ = −2 and dy/dθ = r′sin θ + r cos θ = −1, so the slope is 1/2.

distractorNotes.B: This loses one of the negative signs in the coordinate derivatives.
distractorNotes.D: This reports dr/dθ rather than the Cartesian slope.

items.prompt: The curve r = 3 cos θ is traced once with r ≥ 0 as θ runs from −π/2 to π/2. What is the area it encloses?
items.rationale: Area = (1/2)∫ from −π/2 to π/2 of 9 cos^2 θ dθ = 9π/4. The given interval traces the circle once.

distractorNotes.A: This omits the factor 1/2 in polar area.
distractorNotes.C: This treats 3 as the radius of the Cartesian circle.
distractorNotes.D: This integrates only one half of the enclosed region.

parts.title: Graphing calculator
parts.directions: Select one answer. Numerical choices are rounded as displayed.

items.prompt: A curve is parametrized by x = sin(t^2), y = t^2/2 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2. What is its arc length?
items.rationale: The speed is √[(2t cos(t^2))^2 + t^2] = t√[4 cos^2(t^2) + 1] on t ≥ 0. Numerical integration from 0 to 2 gives 3.506418990.

distractorNotes.A: This gives the distance between the endpoints, not curve length.
distractorNotes.C: This uses the incorrect speed 2t instead of the magnitude of the actual velocity vector.
distractorNotes.D: This inserts an unnecessary factor 1/2 into the arc-length formula.

items.prompt: A particle has velocity v(t) = (e^(−t), sin(t^2)) meters per second, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2. What distance does it travel?
items.rationale: Distance is ∫ from 0 to 2 of √[e^(−2t) + sin^2(t^2)] dt = 1.489014786 m.

distractorNotes.A: This uses only the horizontal displacement.
distractorNotes.B: This is the magnitude of displacement, not distance traveled.

items.prompt: For 0.2 ≤ θ ≤ 1.1, consider the polar region with 2 ≤ r ≤ 2 + sin θ. Both bounding radii are positive on this interval. What is its area?
items.rationale: Since sin θ > 0 on the interval, the outer radius is 2 + sin θ. The area is (1/2)∫ from 0.2 to 1.1 of [(2 + sin θ)^2 − 4] dθ = 1.225556155.

distractorNotes.B: This omits the factor 1/2 in the difference-of-squares formula.
distractorNotes.C: This squares the difference of radii instead of subtracting squared radii.
distractorNotes.D: This includes the inner circular sector as well.

items.prompt: The polar curve r = 1 + 0.3 cos(2θ) is traced once for 0 ≤ θ < 2π, with r always positive. What is the total length, in radians, of the set of angles for which the point is more than 1.2 units from the origin?
items.rationale: Because r > 0, the distance condition is cos(2θ) > 2/3. There are two cosine periods on the θ interval; their total qualifying angular length is 2 arccos(2/3) = 1.682137341.

distractorNotes.A: This counts only half the qualifying angular intervals.
distractorNotes.B: This doubles the qualifying angular measure.
distractorNotes.C: This is the complementary angular measure.

parts.title: Graphing calculator
parts.directions: Show integral or equation setups and justify conclusions.

items.prompt: A plotter moves in a plane with position r(t) = (x(t), y(t)), measured in centimeters, and velocity v(t) = (1 + 0.4 cos(t^2), sin t + 0.2), measured in centimeters per second. Its initial position is r(0) = (0, 1), and 0 ≤ t ≤ 3.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the plotter’s position at t = 3.
steps: Integrate each velocity component and add its initial coordinate.

rubric.criterion: Includes the initial position and obtains x(3).
Obtains y(3) and gives the coordinate pair with units.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the acceleration vector at t = 1 and determine whether speed is increasing or decreasing then. Justify.
steps: Differentiate v: a(t) = (−0.8t sin(t^2), cos t).
Their dot product is −0.255955202 < 0. Since speed is positive, its derivative has the same negative sign.

rubric.criterion: Evaluates the acceleration and correctly computes either the velocity–acceleration dot product or the derivative of speed.
Uses the sign of that dot product or speed derivative to justify decreasing speed.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the total distance traveled from t = 0 to t = 3.
steps: Integrate the magnitude of velocity: ∫ from 0 to 3 of √[(1 + 0.4 cos(t^2))^2 + (sin t + 0.2)^2] dt.

rubric.criterion: Integrates speed over the correct time interval.

items.prompt: Let R be the region inside the polar curve r = 2 cos θ and outside the circle r = 1. Use the tracing interval −π/2 ≤ θ ≤ π/2 for r = 2 cos θ, where its radius is nonnegative and the curve is traced once.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the boundary intersection angles in the given tracing interval. State and justify one continuous angular interval that describes all of R with inner radius 1.
parts.answer: Intersection angles −π/3 and π/3; the interval is [−π/3, π/3].
steps: Solve 2 cos θ = 1 to obtain θ = ±π/3 within the stated tracing interval.
The outer radius is at least 1 exactly when cos θ ≥ 1/2, which holds on [−π/3, π/3].

rubric.criterion: Justifies the interval using 2 cos θ ≥ 1 and the specified single tracing.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the exact area of R.
steps: Area = (1/2)∫ from −π/3 to π/3 of [4 cos^2 θ − 1] dθ.
Since 4 cos^2 θ − 1 = 1 + 2 cos(2θ), the area is (1/2)[θ + sin(2θ)] from −π/3 to π/3 = π/3 + √3/2.

rubric.criterion: Uses outer squared radius minus inner squared radius with factor 1/2.
Uses the correct bounds and a valid antiderivative.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the Cartesian tangent line to r = 2 cos θ at θ = π/4. Verify that the derivative denominator used for the slope is nonzero.
steps: At θ = π/4, r = √2 and the point is (1, 1).
Here r′ = −2 sin θ, so dx/dθ = −4 sin θ cos θ = −2 and dy/dθ = 2(cos^2 θ − sin^2 θ) = 0.

rubric.criterion: Computes both coordinate derivatives and verifies dx/dθ ≠ 0.
